topic: The Power of Combination: Mastering Product and Chain Rules
target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school calculus students

outline.topic: The Power of Combination: Mastering Product and Chain Rules
outline.target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school calculus students

sections.title: Foundation: Derivative as a Rate of Change
sections.content: Briefly revisit the derivative as the instantaneous slope of a tangent line. Introduce the prerequisite: basic power rules and trigonometric derivatives. Establish the challenge: How do we differentiate functions that are multiplied together or nested inside one another?
sections.example: Visualizing a character, 'Calc-Bot', moving along a simple curve y = x^2, where the slope represents his instantaneous velocity.

sections.title: The Product Rule: Growing Areas
sections.content: Explain that the derivative of a product is NOT the product of the derivatives. Use a geometric approach: represent f(x) * g(x) as the area of a rectangle. As x increases, both the width (f) and height (g) grow. The total change in area is the sum of the growth of the two sides.
sections.example: Imagine a rectangular digital garden where width u(x) = x and height v(x) = sin(x). To find the rate of change of the area, we use the formula: d/dx(uv) = u'v + uv'.

sections.title: The Chain Rule: Linked Gears
sections.content: Introduce composite functions f(g(x)). Use the 'Gears' metaphor: if Gear A turns 3 times faster than Gear B, and Gear B turns 2 times faster than Gear C, Gear A turns 3 * 2 = 6 times faster than Gear C. This leads to the formula: dy/dx = (dy/du) * (du/dx).
sections.example: A 'Nested Doll' visual: An outer function (the big doll) contains an inner function (the small doll). To find the change, you must differentiate the big doll while keeping the small one inside, then multiply by the derivative of the small doll.

sections.title: The Synergy: Combining Both Rules
sections.content: Demonstrate a complex scenario where a product contains a composite function. This requires applying the Product Rule first, then using the Chain Rule during the differentiation of the individual terms. Emphasize tracking each 'layer' of the calculation.
sections.example: Calc-Bot is flying a drone. The altitude is h(x) = x^2 * sin(3x). Here, x^2 and sin(3x) are multiplied (Product Rule), but sin(3x) is nested (Chain Rule). The visual shows the calculation branches splitting and then recombining.

sections.title: Interactive Summary & Visual Recap
sections.content: A high-speed visual summary of the two formulas. Contrast them side-by-side: Product Rule = 'Addition of growth components'; Chain Rule = 'Multiplication of rates'. Provide a final mnemonic to help students remember the order of operations.
sections.example: A 30-second animation of the 'Rectangle' and the 'Gears' merging into a single master equation sheet, highlighting the key derivative symbols in bright neon colors.

storyboard.title: Foundation: Derivative as a Rate of Change
lecture_lines: A derivative represents the instantaneous rate of change.
Calc-Bot’s velocity is the slope of the tangent line.
But how do we differentiate products or nested functions?
animations: Calc-Bot (#00FF00) moves along the curve y=x^2 (#1E90FF).
A point on the curve is highlighted, and a tangent line (#FFFF00) appears.
The slope of the tangent line is labeled as the derivative dy/dx (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Product Rule: Growing Areas
lecture_lines: The derivative of a product isn't just multiplying derivatives.
Visualize a rectangle with growing width and height.
The change in area depends on both side's rates.
We add the growth from each side separately.
The rule: derivative of first times second plus vice versa.
animations: A rectangle with width u(x) (#1E90FF) and height v(x) (#FF69B4) represents the area u*v.
The rectangle expands slightly, showing growth increments du and dv at the edges.
Two areas of growth, u*dv and v*du, are highlighted in #FFFF00 and #00FF00.
The Product Rule formula (uv)' = u'v + uv' appears in #FFFFFF.
Substitute u=x and v=sin(x) into the formula to show the derivative calculation.

storyboard.title: The Chain Rule: Linked Gears
lecture_lines: Composite functions are like one gear driving another.
The outer rate multiplies the inner rate of change.
Think of nested dolls: outside first, then the inside.
Differentiate the outer shell, keeping the inner part intact.
Then, multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
animations: Three linked gears (A #FFD700, B #FFA500, C #FF4500) appear to represent nested functions.
Gear A turns, causing Gear B and then Gear C to turn at relative rates.
The ratios dy/du and du/dx appear above the connections between the gears.
The Chain Rule formula dy/dx = (dy/du) * (du/dx) fades in center (#FFFFFF).
A 'Nested Doll' visual shows f(u) as the outer layer and g(x) as the inner layer.

storyboard.title: The Synergy: Combining Both Rules
lecture_lines: Complex functions often require using both rules together.
Start with the Product Rule to split the components.
Apply the Chain Rule when differentiating the nested term.
Track each layer carefully to avoid calculation errors.
Recombine the branches to find the final derivative.
animations: The complex function h(x) = x^2 * sin(3x) appears in #FFFFFF.
The Product Rule splits the function into u=x^2 (#1E90FF) and v=sin(3x) (#FF69B4).
The first term u'v = 2x * sin(3x) is calculated and highlighted.
The second term uv' requires the Chain Rule on sin(3x), yielding x^2 * 3cos(3x).
The full derivative 2x*sin(3x) + 3x^2*cos(3x) is assembled and highlighted in #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: Interactive Summary & Visual Recap
lecture_lines: Product rule adds growth; Chain rule multiplies rates.
Visualize rectangles for products and gears for composition.
Master these patterns to tackle any calculus challenge.
animations: The Product Rule and Chain Rule formulas are displayed side-by-side for comparison.
Rectangle (Product) and Gear (Chain) icons merge into a single 'Calculus Rules' symbol.
A mnemonic 'Add Growth for Products, Multiply Rates for Chains' appears in #00FF00.
